title: The Record of the Udumbara Flower
author: Zhanran
excerpt: The original text is taken from the Chronicle of the Elder Master Xuyun’s Self-Narration, the section “The Record of the Udumbara Flower.”

inline.s: The original text is taken from the Chronicle of the Elder Master Xuyun’s Self-Narration, the section “The Record of the Udumbara Flower.”

The Lotus Sūtra of the Wondrous Dharma says: “Such a wondrous Dharma the Tathāgatas speak only now and then, like the udumbara flower, which appears but once in a while.” This means: the auspicious bloom appears once in three thousand years, and when it appears a golden-wheel king comes forth. The Tathāgata speaks the wondrous Dharma
(the wondrous Dharma of the one vehicle)
only after the three vehicles
(the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of the bodhisattvas)
have been ripened, and the śrāvaka disciples are all given the prophecy of Buddhahood. This flower
(the udumbara flower)
represents the future stage of attainment; hence it is called the auspicious bloom, the omen of what is to come for those who now hear the Dharma.

[Udumbara flower] Translated into Chinese it is “auspicious bloom” or “auspicious response.” The flower is red-yellow in color, growing in the foothills of the Himalayas and in Ceylon and other places. It blooms once every three thousand years, and when it blooms it appears but once. That is why people call anything rare to see and quick to vanish “a flash of the udumbara.” The Commentary on the Words of the Lotus Sūtra says:
“The udumbara flower: this is called the auspicious bloom. It appears once in three thousand years, and when it appears a golden-wheel king comes forth.”
[One vehicle] The one teaching capable of leading beings to Buddhahood.
Dian
(Yunnan)

in the west, Mount Jizu, is the place where Mahākāśyapa keeps the robe and enters absorption. The mountain is several hundred li in circumference, and the spiritual traces and manifestations of the great bodhisattvas are found in many places. Through the Tang, Song, Yuan, and early Ming, the great worthies and eminent monks — Xiaocheng, Ciji, Yuankong, Jianyue, Zongyu, Dacuo, Dandang — one and all dragon-elephants of their time, indeed always held it in triumph. But after successive ages of turmoil, the temple was destroyed in war; after the Xianfeng and Tongzhi
(the Xianfeng and Tongzhi reign eras)

years, the Buddha-Dharma of Yunnan declined to the extreme, until half of this seat of the Way was turned to ashes. Of the temples that remained, none had a good abbot; though nominally they had left home, they had never heard of the three studies
(the study of precepts, the study of meditation, and the study of wisdom)
. And they had wholly lost the deportment of the Saṅgha; the monasteries had degenerated, difficult to describe in full.
[Mahākāśyapa keeps the robe and enters absorption] Mahākāśyapa
holds the robe and bowl of Śākyamuni Buddha and sits upright
in absorption

, awaiting the descent of Maitreya Buddha six thousand seven hundred million years hence, to hand him the Buddha’s robe and bowl. [Dragon and elephant] The dragon and the elephant. In water the dragon’s power is greatest; on land the elephant’s power is greatest; hence “dragon and elephant” is used as a metaphor for the practitioner of fierce effort who is possessed of the greatest ability.
At the end of the Qing dynasty, when the Venerable Xu Gong, the Chan master Deqing
(Master Xuyun)
, came to pay reverence to the first patriarch

(because Chan was first transmitted by Śākyamuni Buddha to the venerable Mahākāśyapa, he is the first patriarch of Chan; the venerable Bodhidharma is the twenty-eighth patriarch, and the first patriarch of Chan in China)
, at that time there was not a single place on the whole mountain to lodge a visiting monk
(then, though there were many temples on the whole mountain, there was not one place that would put up a monk arriving from outside)
. The Master sighed that the first patriarch’s seat of the Way, its clan-style fallen, its vinaya and teachings unheard
(the vinaya and the scriptures utterly unknown)
, and so he made a vow to revive a ten-direction monastery
(thereupon he vowed to revive a monastery into a ten-direction monastery)
, to be a model for the whole mountain. Thereupon
yuán
, meaning “thereupon”)
, on the site of the old Boyuan Shrine below Boyu Peak, he cleared the mountain and broke the soil, and began
zhào
, meaning “to begin”)
to build the Huguo Zhusheng Chan Temple. In a few years it was completed, and the monastic rules were put in order. That year he entered the capital
(Beijing)
to request the canon
(that year he went to the capital to request the Great Treasury of Scriptures)
, and was graciously granted the purple robe and a tablet inscribed by imperial command, and, in obedience to the decree, returned to the mountain.
[Monastery] A Chan temple; later used generally for any temple.
[Ten-direction monastery]
A temple that widely invites celebrated worthies and eminent monks from all quarters to be abbot, without allowing disciples to inherit the office.
[Descendants’ temple]

In contrast with the “ten-direction monastery,” its property is privately owned by a single monk or by a lineage of monks, unlike the ten-direction monastery, which belongs to the whole community of monks in the world.
[Graciously granted the purple robe]
“The imperial decree
(the emperor’s decree)

: The Yingxiang Temple at Boyu Peak on Mount Jizu in Yunnan is further conferred the name Huguo Zhusheng Chan Temple; the Dragon Treasury (the canon) is graciously bestowed, together with a complete imperial equipage. The imperial command appoints the abbot, and by imperial grace the purple robe, bowl and implements, the jade seal, the staff and the wish-fulfilling scepter are conferred. The abbot Xuyun is posthumously conferred the title ‘Great Master of Buddha-Compassion and Vast Dharma.’”
That year
, the Master ascended the seat and, for the assembly, lectured on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra. Before the hall, the old chestnut
(the ancient chestnut tree)
suddenly put forth several dozen udumbara flowers, as large as a basin, shaped like the lotus
(the lotus
qú
, another name for the water-lily)

, yellow in color like gold, enfolding fragrant stamens, hollow within and pure in substance, not withering for several months — those who saw them called it extraordinary. At Jizu Mountain, the Buddha-Dharma had long gone unheard; now suddenly it was heard, just as the udumbara too appears but once — its auspicious response is inconceivable.
In the Ming
(the Ming dynasty)

, when Master Hanshan had not yet left home, a plantain was set in the courtyard and it drew forth a single golden lotus-flower, which did not wither for three months; afterward he in fact became a teacher of gods and humans. And when he moved to Yue
(Guangdong)
, he revived the sixth patriarch’s seat of the Way and established a Dharma assembly at the Faxing Temple, and in the courtyard
(the courtyard)
there again welled up a single golden lotus.

Usually, when the Way of Dharma arises, there must be an auspicious response to be its omen. The ancient worthies and eminent monks, whose radiance shone through sun and moon and whose Way covered the world
(the world)
, are far too many to recount. Before the sixth patriarch came forth, the bodhi tree had already been planted beside the ordination altar; before Kumārajīva arrived, the connected-tree suddenly
jù
grew in the hall and pavilion. These auspicious responses are attested in the scriptures
(they are clearly evidenced in the scriptures)
[Before the sixth patriarch came forth, the bodhi tree had already been planted beside the ordination altar] During the Liu-Song (420–479 CE)
era,
the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra
founded
an ordination altar at the Faxing Temple in Guangzhou and erected a stele saying:
Hereafter a bodhisattva of the flesh-body (a living bodhisattva) will receive the precepts at this place.

Later, in the first year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty (502), the Tripitaka Master Zhiyao came by sea from Western India and planted a bodhi tree from that land beside this altar, and also foretold:

A hundred and seventy years hence, a bodhisattva of the flesh-body will, beneath this tree, expound the supreme vehicle, deliver countless beings, and be the King of Dharma who truly transmits the Buddha’s mind-seal.
And the sixth patriarch Huineng was precisely
at this time at
this
precept
altar, receiving the complete precepts, and beneath the bodhi tree beside this altar began transmitting the Buddha’s mind-seal.
Hence
his disciples
his
recorded sayings
and called it the Platform Sūtra

[Mind-seal] “Mind” is the Buddha-mind; “seal” has the meaning of approval and confirmation. Chan does not establish words and does not rely on speech; it transmits mind with mind only, using the Buddha-mind to seal and confirm the minds of sentient beings, realizing the mark of non-duality.
[Before Kumārajīva arrived, the connected-tree suddenly grew in the hall and pavilion] In the third year of the Hongshi era of Yao Xing, the Later Qin emperor (

), a connected tree (branches and trunk growing together from two separate roots) grew in the broad courtyard, and the green scallions in the Xiaoyao Garden were in a single night transformed into fragrant herbs (
zhǐ

). The grand astrologer foretold that a great-worthied sage would enter the Central Land. Therefore the Later Qin ruler Yao Xing regarded this as an auspicious omen that a great wise one was about to arrive, and sent an envoy to the state of Liang to respectfully invite Master Kumārajīva; but because the Later Liang ruler obstructed the way, it could not be accomplished. Yao Xing dispatched troops to attack Liangzhou, and the Liang ruler Lü Long was defeated and surrendered; only then was Yao Xing able to bring Master Kumārajīva into the Central Land.

When Master Xu lectured on the sūtra, the old chestnut put forth udumbara flowers; when he transmitted the precepts at Yunqi, a withered plum again opened lotus buds. His name is the same as Hanshan’s
(Master Xuyun’s style-name is Deqing, and Master Hanshan’s style-name is also Deqing)
, and the two auspicious responses are also the same. The Deqing of today — how do we know he is not the Deqing of old? Only the wise know his root and his traces; and this foretells
bǔ
, meaning “to foretell”)
our Dian
(Yunnan)
Buddha-Dharma’s flourishing, which will be as it was before the Yuan and Ming.

[The Deqing of today — how do we know he is not the Deqing of old? Only the wise know his root and his traces] How do we know that the present-day Master Xuyun is not the Hanshan of old? His ground and his manifest traces are known only to the wise! Because Master Xuyun shares the name of Master Hanshan and their deeds are similar, there has long been the saying that Master Xuyun is a reincarnation of Master Hanshan:
The earlier Deqing, the later Deqing — the manifest traces differ, yet the one true body.
When Master Xuyun burned incense and bowed before the flesh-body image of Master Hanshan, he too said:

The Deqing of today, the Deqing of old — now and of old we meet, having changed our forms. The rise and fall of the Buddha-Dharma waits on the season; entering the grove, entering the grass, I never cease.
[Root and traces] The ground and the manifested traces. The Dharma-body bodhisattvas from the first ground
upward
and the Buddhas, from their own true body, transform into many response-bodies in order to deliver sentient beings. Their true body is the ground; the response-bodies are the manifested traces
[The rise and fall of the Buddha-Dharma waits on the season
entering the grove, entering the grass, I never cease]
Whether the Buddha-Dharma is flourishing or decaying, he always
works as ox and horse
and in the mountains and the wilds
ceaselessly
bustles
about
; wherever there are sentient beings, wherever there is suffering, there he goes to
deliver them
Presently the abbot of Zhusheng, the Venerable Shengkong, asked me for a composition, and so I made this eulogy:

The Buddhas’ coming forth in the world is hard to meet, / To hear the Buddha-Dharma is harder still to gain; / Like the udumbara’s surpassing wondrous flower, / That blooms but once through three thousand years.

The phoenix comes not, the River yields no chart; / The sage laments, “My task is done at last.” / The beings of the five turbidities have mighty karmic power; / Without the Buddha’s awe and virtue, who can cast it out?
[The phoenix comes not, the River yields no chart; the sage laments, “My task is done at last.”]
The Master said:
The phoenix comes not, the River brings forth no map; my course is ended.
The Analects, Book of Zihan
) Translation
: Confucius said: The phoenix no longer comes, and from the Yellow River the diagram of the eight trigrams no longer appears. My life, then, is done
[River Map] It is said that the River Map was the basis on which Fu Xi made the earlier-eight trigrams:
“Fu Xi’s making of the eight trigrams was obtained from the River Map.”

Receiving the Buddha’s commendation, the sages and saints / Transform through kalpa after kalpa, dust after dust; / Though empty space be bounded, the vow is not; / Self-awakening, waking others, the awakening-work is whole.
[Kalpa after kalpa, dust after dust]

This describes an extremely, extremely long span of time. The allusion comes from the “dust-kalpa.” The dust-kalpa is also called the dust-point kalpa. [Dust-point kalpa] First, it refers to the three-thousand dust-point kalpa: grind all the things of a three-thousand great-thousand world into ink, and set down a point for each three-thousand great-thousand world passed through; when the ink runs out, all the worlds passed through are again ground into fine dust, and then each fine dust is counted as a kalpa — this is a metaphor showing how extremely long ago the Buddha Great Penetrating Wisdom-Surpassing (Dābhūñña-jñānābhibhū) appeared in the world. Second, it refers to the five-hundred dust-point kalpa: grind five hundred thousand myriad koṭi nayuta asamkhya three-thousand great-thousand worlds into fine dust, and set down one fine dust for each five hundred thousand myriad koṭi nayuta asamkhya lands passed through; when the dust is exhausted, all the worlds passed through are again ground into fine dust, and each fine dust is counted as a kalpa — this is a metaphor showing how extremely long ago Śākyamuni Tathāgata attained Buddhahood.

Therefore, when a bodhisattva spreads the Dharma, / An auspicious response must shine before him; / Hanshan twice saw the golden lotus-flower, / Its light bright as the sun and moon, covering the world.

The Elder Xuyun came to Yunnan to revive the ancient temple, / Twice saw the udumbara bloom upon the ancient tree; / Coming again by vow, the bodhisattva’s practice — / Merit complete in myriad deeds, spreading the six pāramitās.

The first patriarch’s seat at Jizu Mountain, / The Chan wind desolate, decayed to the utmost; / In this end-age he meets the world to carry on the lamp of the patriarchs; / Through hardship, relying only on the power of compassion and vow.
[The lamp of the patriarchs] The Dharma-lamp of the successive patriarchs.
It describes
the patriarchs of successive generations, master
and disciple
succeeding one another, like a lamp-fire that continues without break.
At Yunqi, awaiting the arrival of the supreme person
(the person of the highest attainment)
; at Jizu, a thousand sages are yet to come forth.
In the autumn, the ninth month, of the gēng-xū year
, the bodhisattva-precept disciple Zhang Puhongxi respectfully composed and wrote this.
